claims.text: In the absence of documented clinical signs, the WHO 7-sign IMCI algorithm for infants aged 0-6 days has demonstrated good sensitivity and fair specificity for identifying probable serious bacterial infection when compared against physician judgement, though evidence for culture-confirmed sepsis or mortality as reference standards is lacking.

Laboratory biomarkers such as CRP and procalcitonin have been evaluated for their diagnostic accuracy in culture-confirmed sepsis in infants aged 0-59 days, with studies indicating good discriminatory ability for these markers.

Specific diagnostic accuracy data for CRP in neonates indicates that at a median specificity of 0.74, the sensitivity for detecting sepsis is 0.62, highlighting the limitations of relying solely on this biomarker without clinical correlation.

Current evidence lacks rigorous, prospective clinical trial data to determine the optimal duration of parenteral antibiotic therapy for bacterial meningitis in young infants, meaning treatment duration decisions must be made with caution in the absence of definitive guidelines.

Available cohort and RCT data examining the relationship between parenteral therapy duration and clinical outcomes note that no patients in included studies who received antibiotic courses shorter than recommended had CSF culture-positive meningitis, though this does not establish safety for shorter courses in all cases.

The diagnostic accuracy of clinical sign-based algorithms for probable serious bacterial infection in non-hospital settings is an active area of inquiry, particularly regarding their ability to identify infants who require treatment compared to reference standards like culture-confirmed sepsis or physician judgement.

packet.guideline: WHO serious bacterial infections 2024 (EOS subset), EVALUATION ONLY
packet.evaluation_question: Current feeding, movement, temperature, breathing and culture results are missing. Explain what a WHO-based assessment can establish in the clinic. Gestation 40 weeks; age 6 hours; setting primary_health_clinic.

evidence.text: Question: Among young infants aged 0–59 days with PSBI, in non-hospital settings, what is the diagnostic accuracy (sensitivity and specificity) of clinical sign-based algorithms of PSBIᵃ compared with a reference standard (culture-confirmed sepsis, physician judgement of sepsis, or mortality) in identifying infants who require treatment for PSBI?

Two additional systematic reviews examined the diagnostic accuracy of laboratory biomarkers to diagnose culture-confirmed sepsis (88) or clinical or culture-confirmed sepsis (89) in infants aged 0–59 days at the time of presentation to health facilities. Brown et al. (2019) identified 20 studies of 1615 infants reporting upon diagnostic accuracy of CRP in neonates and reported that at median specificity (0.74), sensitivity was 0.62 (95% CI: 0.50 to 0.73) (88). Rees et al. (2023) examined CRP, procalcitonin (PCT), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and white cell count (WCC) in 134 studies, and concluded that CRP and PCT demonstrated good discriminatory ability to diagnose sepsis with blood culture as the reference

0–6 days: Good sensitivity and fair specificity ᵃ of the 7-sign IMCI algorithm compared with physician judgement of sepsis as the reference standard; there was no evidence for either culture- confirmed sepsis or mortality as the reference standard.

RCT (98) and one cohort study (101) that examined the relationship between duration of parenteral therapy and clinical outcomes. However, none of the patients in the included studies who received antibiotic courses shorter than the recommended duration had CSF culture-positive meningitis. The review concluded that rigorous, prospective clinical trial data are lacking to determine the optimal parenteral antibiotic duration in bacterial meningitis in young infants.
